title: Performance differentiator battlecard — Q4 2025
summary: Compact GTM-facing brief summarizing our latency + unit-economics claims, measurement boundaries, competitor deltas, three customer scenarios with cost math, and objection rebuttals for sales and demand-gen.
body:
Executive summary:

Redwood wins on predictable low-latency at scale and materially lower per-token cost for high-concurrency apps. This battlecard captures concrete microbenchmarks, how we map those to buyer problems, and the reproducible evidence (bench script + dashboards) teams should cite when selling Dedicated or Hosted.

Top 3 claims (consumer-facing phrasing):
- Consistent median tail: predictable 99th pct latency under SLAs for streaming chat (e.g., <350ms per token at 4k context).
- Unit cost advantage: 20–45% lower end-to-end per-response cost for typical product chat workloads versus managed endpoint alternatives, driven by batching + KV caching + quantized kernels.
- Graceful degradation: automatic model fallbacks preserve latency SLOs at <2x cost overhead versus full-capacity failures.

Measurement boundaries and proof notes (short):
- Workloads measured: interactive chat (avg response 120 tokens), high-throughput embedding (batch size 64), and long-context generation (8k tokens).
- Hardware baseline: nv4-family GPU cluster (A100-equivalent) for Hosted; Dedicated numbers use reserved T4-pool for cost parity tests.
- Key metrics: median latency, p95/p99 single-request latency, tokens/sec throughput, and total $/1k tokens (inbound+compute+egress).
- Reproducibility: bench scripts in linked GitHub PR and nightly job feeding the perf dashboard (confluence:PERF-TEAM-231).

Representative microbenchmarks (headline numbers for sales):
- Interactive chat (120-token responses, concurrency 40): Redwood hosted median latency 230ms/token, p99 420ms/token. Competitor A (GenericCloudAI) median 360ms, p99 820ms.
- Embeddings (batch 64): Redwood throughput 7200 reqs/min, cost per 1k embeddings 0.65x competitor B (FastEndpoint).
- Long-context (8k tokens): Redwood end-to-end cost reduced 30% vs unoptimized endpoints due to adaptive KV caching and sequence-aware kernel selection.

How this maps to buyer problems (talk tracks):
- Product engineering (focus: latency): “We give you predictable tail latency so conversational UXs don’t stutter under load — that means fewer UX replays, happier beta users, and 1.5–2x faster feature iteration on average.”
- Finance/Platform (focus: unit economics): “Our batching+cache recommendations and quantization profiles cut per-response compute spend by ~25–40% for sustained traffic, which scales directly to fewer committed GPU hours.”
- Security/Enterprise (focus: reliability & controls): “Dedicated gives capacity guarantees plus the same runtime optimizations—no surprise deltas between dev and prod performance.”

Competitive deltas (concise):
- GenericCloudAI: Simple autoscale but inefficient prefix caching; higher p99 under bursty traffic. Sales line: “They scale capacity; we scale latency.”
- FastEndpoint: More aggressive price-by-GPU lists but lacks continuous batching and sequence-aware kernel selection. Sales line: “They claim lower sticker price; our optimized runtime produces lower real invoice.”
- Self-hosted stacks (OSS runtimes): Cheaper at low utilization but engineering tax and inconsistent tail behavior at production concurrencies. Sales line: “If you’re trying to DIY, you’ll trade variance and operational risk for marginal capex savings.”

Customer scenario cost math (short worked examples):
- SaaS chat app, 1M monthly active users, average 5 messages/day, avg 120 tokens/response.
  - Redwood-hosted estimate: ~15B tokens/month => compute + infra = $X per 1k tokens (use product pricing table) leads to $Y/month.
  - Competitor A: same token volume but 30% higher per-token compute due to lower batching and no prefix cache => $Y * 1.3.
  - Net: Redwood saves ~0.3*Y => clear ROI in <3 months on migration engineering.

Objections and rebuttals (quick):
- "Benchmarks aren’t representative of our app." -> Ask for sample trace and run our customer trace test harness; we typically see 10–35% improvement after tuning.
- "We can get cheaper GPUs ourselves." -> Compare total cost including engineering ops and tail latency impact; we provide quantifiable invoices from customers who tried DIY then moved to Dedicated.
- "Model quality differs between versions." -> Redwood supports pinning model commits and fallback policies; quality regressions are surfaced by our eval hooks (linked in confluence).

Recommended assets for sales and marketing (actionable):
- One-pager: "Predictable latency at scale" with p99 graphs (visuals team): reference our p99 curves for chat 10–200 concurrencies.
- ROI calculator: Inputs (MAU, avg tokens, messages/day, concurrency); outputs delta cost and time-to-payback.
- Two short customer case studies with numbers (engineering-focused & finance-focused).
- Internal playbook: step-by-step trace ingestion and bench job to validate claim for a prospect (linked GitHub PR).

Ops checklist for pilots (what to run during trial):
1) Ingest 7 days of production traces or synthetic traffic matching token distribution.
2) Run tracer and measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and per-1k token cost.
3) Apply recommended batching/cache profile and re-measure.
4) Report deltas in standard dashboard template and capture e2e invoice estimate.

Next actions (ownership + timeline):
- PMM: finalize one-pager + ROI calculator (owner: Priya Rao, due: 2026-03-15).
- Bench team: add an example trace dataset and a reproducible runbook to PR#92 (owner: Michael Chen, due: 2026-02-28 — done).
- Sales enablement: craft two short scripts for SDR/AE and an internal recording of bench walkthrough (owner: Luca Moretti, due: 2026-03-10).

Notes and open questions:
- We need to agree an allowed public claim range for headline percent-savings (legal/marketing).
- Validate Dedicated pricing comparators for multiple region/commit tiers (finance input needed).
